headline: New moon springs reopen the sunset striper window from Kings Point to Execution Rocks
subhead: After a sluggish, bunker-heavy week of daytime lockjaw, building tides and a converging evening flood set up the best striper window since the June full moon.
body_markdown:
Last week the Sound gave us exactly what mid-summer neap tides usually give us: warm, slick water, plenty of bait, and bass that wanted no part of daylight. Little Neck Bay and Manhasset Bay have been running hot on the surface — I don't have a hard number but it felt like bathwater on top, the kind of warmth that pushes stripers down and out rather than up and in. A weak system rolled through midweek and put a little chop on the water for a day, nothing that really turned things over, just enough to dirty the surface film off Matinecock for 24 hours before it laid back down. The moon's been waning toward new, which means the tides have been running small — slow current at Execution Rocks, slack water sitting around too long at Stepping Stones, and bass that had no reason to commit to any one piece of structure.

That changes this week. New moon lands Saturday, and with it come the spring tides — bigger swings, faster current, more water moving through the pinch points that make this zone what it is. The piece I'm circling on the calendar is Friday through Monday, when the PM flood tide starts converging with sunset at Kings Point. That's the first evening window we've had like this since the June full moon, and it's the kind of alignment that turns a mediocre bay into a striper highway for about ninety minutes a night. Bigger tides also mean more bait getting flushed out of the back bays and funneled past Hart Island and through the Throgs Neck pinch — that's going to wake fish up that have been sitting on bunker schools all week without really feeding.

Speaking of bunker — they're stacked up off Matinecock Point again, thick pods sitting just off the point in 15 to 20 feet, and where there's bunker in July there's usually something under them. Problem is, most of the action on those schools has been early — first light, before the boat traffic and jet skis push everything down. I've had reports of bass and blues shadowing the pods at dawn, then going quiet by 8 AM once the sun gets up and the water flattens out. If you're going to work that bunker school, get there before the sun clears the trees, snag one on a weighted treble and freeline it back into the school, or run a bunker spoon on wire behind the boat at a slow troll. By mid-morning it's mostly just bait balls with nothing interested.

Execution Rocks is still doing what Execution Rocks does — it's just been on a smaller clock with these neap tides. The outgoing has been the better stage, current sweeping bait off the rockpile and down toward the channel, and guys working bunker chunks on fish-finder rigs or bouncing bucktails tipped with white Gulp along the down-current side have picked at schoolie-to-mid-30-inch bass. Nothing blitz-worthy, but steady if you're patient and fish the full stage of the outgoing rather than just the first hour. Stepping Stones has been similar — a slower current window meant fish were sitting in the eddies rather than stacked on the current lane, so drifting live eels or bunker chunks right along the edge of the light's rockpile, letting them sit rather than working them hard, has been the better play. Once these spring tides kick in this weekend, I expect both spots to tighten up and get more predictable — faster water means fish committing to ambush points instead of loafing.

Fluke have been an interesting story. The bay water's gotten warm enough on the surface that the fluke have been sliding out of the shallow flats in Manhasset Bay and Hempstead Harbor and setting up on the deeper channel edges — 25 to 35 feet off Hart Island and along the Throgs Neck Bridge drift. That's actually produced some decent action, fish to 4 and 5 pounds on white Gulp Swimming Mullets rigged on ¾-ounce bucktails, dragged slow on the last of the outgoing where the current stacks bait against the channel wall. If you've been fishing the shallow grass flats and coming up empty this week, that warm surface layer is your answer — the fish didn't leave, they just went down and out.

Porgies have been the reliable bread-and-butter this month — Hart Island reef and the rockpile at Execution Rocks are both holding good numbers, sandworms or clam on a hi-lo rig in 20 to 30 feet, best on the last two hours of the incoming when the current's still got some push but isn't ripping. Weakfish, I'll be honest, are a non-story again this year — water's plenty warm enough on paper, but I haven't had or heard of a single credible report out of this zone, and I'm not going to pretend otherwise. Warm water alone doesn't bring weakfish back; something else has to click, and it hasn't in years.

If I had one shot this week, I'd take the Saturday or Sunday evening flood at Kings Point or the Stepping Stones light, right as the tide peaks into sunset. That's the alignment the calendar's been building toward, and building spring tides plus low light plus a concentration of bait is about as good a striper setup as this zone offers in July. Plan B if the wind kicks up out of the southwest and muddies the surface — fall back to the fluke drift along Throgs Neck in that deeper water, where the fish don't care as much what's happening on top.
